questions.subject: ANTHROPOLOGY
questions.topic: Human evolution and the fossil record
questions.learningObjective: examine fossil record using anthropological evidence

stimulus.body: A cave sequence in East Africa yields layered ash beds, a jaw with worn molars, and stone flakes, each sealed between dated volcanic horizons.

questions.stem: Which statement about fossil record is best supported by the account?

options.text: The fossil record preserves remains in stratified deposits whose dates and contexts allow scientists to reconstruct relative ages and ancient environments.
The fossil record is a complete and unbiased sample of every species that has ever lived on Earth.
options.misconception: The ash layers and sealed finds let researchers place the jaw and tools in a dated sequence.

options.text: The fossil record can only be interpreted when a complete skeleton is found in a single layer.
options.misconception: It assumes completeness, whereas the record is famously partial and shaped by preservation bias.

options.text: The fossil record consists of written accounts of animals made by early naturalists.
options.misconception: It imposes an impossible standard of complete skeletons, ignoring fragmentary but informative finds.

questions.explanation: It confuses fossils with written descriptions, a different kind of evidence.
questions.hint: Stratigraphic context and associated dates turn isolated finds into evidence about change over time.

questions.subject: ANTHROPOLOGY
questions.topic: Human evolution and the fossil record
questions.learningObjective: examine hominin using anthropological evidence

stimulus.body: A researcher describes a fossil whose teeth and jaw suggest a lineage closely related to humans but not to chimpanzees after their split.

questions.stem: The evidence most strongly supports which claim about hominin?

options.text: A hominin is any primate that happens to live on the ground rather than in trees.
options.misconception: The fossil belongs to the human lineage after its divergence from the lineage leading to chimpanzees.

options.text: A hominin is a member of the lineage that includes humans and our extinct relatives after the split from the chimpanzee line.
A hominin is a fossil that has been classified as a species of great ape.
options.misconception: It broadens the term to any terrestrial primate, which would include many non-human lineages.

options.text: A hominin is a human being who lived during the last ten thousand years only.
options.misconception: It reverses the relationship by calling the fossil an ape rather than a human-lineage member.

questions.explanation: It restricts the term to very recent humans, excluding the long earlier history of the lineage.
questions.hint: Membership in the hominin lineage is defined by evolutionary history, not by habitat or recency.

questions.subject: ANTHROPOLOGY

questions.learningObjective: examine bipedalism using anthropological evidence

questions.subject: ANTHROPOLOGY
questions.topic: Human evolution and the fossil record
questions.learningObjective: examine hominin using anthropological evidence

stimulus.body: A researcher describes a fossil whose teeth and jaw suggest a lineage closely related to humans but not to chimpanzees after their split.

questions.stem: How should hominin be understood in this context?

options.text: A hominin is any primate that happens to live on the ground rather than in trees.
options.misconception: The fossil belongs to the human lineage after its divergence from the lineage leading to chimpanzees.

options.text: A hominin is a member of the lineage that includes humans and our extinct relatives after the split from the chimpanzee line.
A hominin is a fossil that has been classified as a species of great ape.
options.misconception: It broadens the term to any terrestrial primate, which would include many non-human lineages.

options.text: A hominin is a human being who lived during the last ten thousand years only.
options.misconception: It reverses the relationship by calling the fossil an ape rather than a human-lineage member.

questions.explanation: It restricts the term to very recent humans, excluding the long earlier history of the lineage.
questions.hint: Membership in the hominin lineage is defined by evolutionary history, not by habitat or recency.

questions.subject: ANTHROPOLOGY
questions.topic: Human evolution and the fossil record
questions.learningObjective: examine bipedalism using anthropological evidence

stimulus.body: A pelvis and knee joint from a young fossil show a bowl-shaped hip and an angled femur suited to walking on two legs.

questions.stem: What is the best reading of bipedalism here?

options.text: Bipedalism is a form of movement that humans share equally with quadrupedal apes.
options.misconception: The hip and knee anatomy indicates habitual upright walking in this individual.

options.text: Bipedalism describes the habit of climbing trees using all four limbs.
options.misconception: It equates bipedalism with traits of four-legged apes, which is the opposite anatomical pattern.

options.text: Bipedalism is walking on two legs and is a defining early adaptation of the human lineage.
Bipedalism is a term for the large brain that distinguishes modern humans.
options.misconception: It confuses upright walking with climbing, a different locomotor adaptation.

questions.explanation: It substitutes brain size for locomotion, mixing two separate characteristics.
questions.hint: Bipedal anatomy appears early in hominin evolution, before large brain size.

questions.subject: ANTHROPOLOGY
questions.topic: Human evolution and the fossil record
questions.learningObjective: examine Australopithecus using anthropological evidence

stimulus.body: A small-brained fossil from southern Africa combines a upright posture with ape-sized teeth and a face adapted to heavy chewing.

questions.stem: Which account of Australopithecus is most consistent with the facts?

options.text: Australopithecus is a genus of large-brained humans that appeared only after modern humans.
options.misconception: The fossil combines upright walking with a small brain and powerful jaws typical of the genus.

options.text: Australopithecus is a type of African great ape that walked on four legs.
options.misconception: It reverses the chronology, placing the genus after modern humans rather than long before.

options.text: Australopithecus is the name of a single famous fossil individual rather than a whole genus.
options.misconception: It misclassifies a bipedal hominin as a non-bipedal ape.

options.text: Australopithecus is an early hominin genus showing bipedalism with a relatively small brain and robust chewing adaptations.

questions.explanation: It confuses a genus with one specimen, a common but important error.
questions.hint: The mix of bipedal and ape-like traits is the hallmark of these early hominins.
